title: An LLM-in-the-loop RL Framework for Bioinformatics Feature Selection

paper.title: An LLM-in-the-loop RL Framework for Bioinformatics Feature Selection
paper.abstract:
Abstract High-dimensional bioinformatics data, characterized by a large number of features relative to the number of samples, pose major challenges such as the “curse of dimensionality,” leading to overfitting, high computational cost, and poor generalization.
Traditional feature selection methods often suffer from limited scalability and adaptability in such domains.
We propose an LLM-in-the-loop reinforcement learning (RL) framework for bioinformatics feature selection, where the RL agent formulates feature selection as a sequential decision-making task, while the large language model (LLM) enhances the process in two ways: (1) guiding exploration through domain-informed advice, and (2) providing hybrid rewards that integrate data-driven performance with knowledge-driven evaluation.
The LLM also produces explanations to improve interpretability for human experts without altering the RL policy update.
Experiments on diverse bioinformatics datasets show that the LLM-in-the-loop framework outperforms baselines, achieves stable performance across downstream models, and converges faster than pure RL.

Traditional feature selection methods often suffer from limited scalability and adaptability in such domains. We propose an LLM-in-the-loop reinforcement learning (RL) framework for bioinformatics feature selection, where the RL agent formulates feature selection as a sequential decision-making task, while the large language model (LLM) enhances the process in two ways: (1) guiding exploration through domain-informed advice, and (2) providing hybrid rewards that integrate data-driven performance with knowledge-driven evaluation. Keywords: Feature Selection, Large Language Models, Reinforcement Learning, LLM in the Loop. I Introduction With advances in data collection, high-dimensional data have become increasingly common and challenging, particularly in bioinformatics [ 1 ] . Such datasets often contain tens of thousands of features but only a few hundred samples in practice, giving rise to the well-known “curse of dimensionality.” This leads to two major challenges: (1) models are likely to overfit, as noisy correlations can outweigh true biological signals, and (2) computational costs grow rapidly, which makes model training expensive [ 2 ] . For example, genomic or molecular datasets may require processing the full set of descriptors, which will slow down both model development and clinical translation. Feature selection is therefore essential to remove irrelevant or redundant features [ 3 ] . Beyond reducing complexity, selecting a biologically meaningful feature subset (e.g., key genes or biomarkers) improves predictive performance and enhances interpretability for downstream biomedical analysis and clinical research. Fig. 1 shows how feature selection reduces downstream task processing time while boosting performance on a myocardial infarction dataset. Fig. 1 : Feature selection brings fewer key features to improve downstream performance and reduce processing time. Traditional feature selection approaches fall into three categories: filter, wrapper, and embedded [ 4 ] . Filter methods (e.g., Fisher Score [ 5 ] , Information Gain [ 6 ] , Chi-Square Test [ 7 ] ) evaluate features individually before model training. They are efficient but ignore feature interactions, which often leads to missing informative combinations. Wrapper methods assess subsets using the performance of a predictive model [ 4 ] . While typically more accurate, they are expensive for high-dimensional datasets, since a new model must be trained for each subset. Embedded methods integrate selection into model training, such as Lasso regularization [ 8 ] and its extensions [ 9 ] , which enforce sparsity in parameters. These balance efficiency and accuracy, but remain model-dependent and lack generality across domains. Fig. 2 : Overview of the LLM-in-the-loop reinforcement learning framework for feature selection. Reinforcement Learning (RL) offers a new view on feature selection [ 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 ] . It frames feature selection as a sequential decision process for each feature. An RL agent learns through trial and error to find the best feature subset. Compared to traditional methods, RL can perform a more global search and adapt to changing data environments. RL shows great potential but faces two main challenges. First, exploration within large feature spaces is inefficient. The vast number of possible feature combinations makes a purely “blind” search slow and unlikely to identify the best solution. Second, reward signals are limited by predefined metrics. In RL-based feature selection, rewards are usually derived from human-defined performance metrics, which may not fully capture domain relevance or real-world utility. To address these challenges, we propose an LLM-in-the-loop RL framework that treats LLMs as domain experts to assist the agent. First, LLM as Decision Maker: The LLM uses its extensive domain knowledge, narrows the exploration space by suggesting promising features, and at each step advises whether the current feature should be selected. Second, LLM as Reviewer: The LLM provides feedback after each decision, producing a hybrid reward that combines the LLM’s knowledge-driven evaluation with the policy’s data-driven performance. This mitigates the bias of conventional reward and offers the agent a richer and more realistic learning signal. In addition, the LLM generates natural-language explanations of its advice and reviews, which, while not part of the RL loop, enhance interpretability for human experts. Experiments in bioinformatics domains verify the framework. The results show that it achieves the best or second-best performance in most tasks, with improvements of up to 4% in classification accuracy and a lower regression error compared to baselines. In addition, convergence analysis indicates that the LLM-in-the-loop framework achieves comparable performance more quickly, and ablation results confirm the value of LLM guidance in both decision-making and reward shaping. II LLM-in-the-Loop RL Framework II-A Background and Task Feature selection is important in high-dimensional bioinformatics tasks, where datasets often contain thousands of candidate features but only limited samples. Using all features may introduce noise and redundancy, increase computational cost, and reduce model interpretability. Let 𝑫 = ( 𝑿 , 𝒚 ) \bm{D}=(\bm{X},\bm{y}) denote a supervised dataset, where 𝑿 ∈ ℝ n × d \bm{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} contains n n samples and d d features, and 𝒚 \bm{y} denotes the labels or regression targets. The goal is to select a compact subset S ⊆ { 1 , … , d } S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\} and train a downstream model on 𝑿 S \bm{X}_{S} , so that prediction performance is improved while redundancy and complexity are reduced. Feature selection is combinatorial, since the number of possible subsets grows exponentially with d d . RL provides a sequential formulation by deciding whether to select or skip each candidate feature. However, pure RL may explore inefficiently and rely only on task-driven reward signals. We therefore introduce LLM guidance into the RL loop, combining RL-based optimization with LLM-based knowledge about feature relevance, redundancy, and semantic consistency. II-B Proposed Method Our framework integrates three LLM-assisted modules into the RL-based feature selection process: an LLM filter, an LLM decision maker, and an LLM reviewer. The LLM filter first builds a candidate priority list based on feature names, statistical summaries, and available domain descriptions. This step is used to prioritize exploration rather than permanently discard low-ranked features, so the RL agent can still discover useful but non-obvious candidates. As shown in Fig. 2 , the RL agent sequentially interacts with the environment. At each step, the agent observes the current selected subset and the current candidate feature. Before making a decision, it queries the LLM decision maker, which outputs an action advice score indicating whether the candidate feature is promising. The RL agent combines this score with its own policy to take an action. After the action is executed, the environment provides downstream validation feedback, and the LLM reviewer provides an additional knowledge-driven evaluation. These signals are combined into a hybrid reward. The LLM does not directly determine the final feature subset. Instead, it acts as a soft guide for exploration and reward shaping. The final policy is still learned by the RL agent using task-driven validation feedback. The LLM also produces short natural-language explanations for human interpretability, but these explanations are not used in policy updates. II-C Reinforcement Learning Framework We formalize feature selection as a Markov Decision Process ( 𝒮 , 𝒜 , 𝒫 , R , γ ) (\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},\mathcal{P},R,\gamma) : • State s t ∈ 𝒮 s_{t}\in\mathcal{S} : the current selected subset, represented as a binary vector 𝒙 t ∈ { 0 , 1 } d \bm{x}_{t}\in\{0,1\}^{d} , together with the current candidate feature. • Action a t ∈ 𝒜 a_{t}\in\mathcal{A} : a binary decision for the current feature, i.e., a t ∈ { select , skip } a_{t}\in\{\text{select},\text{skip}\} . • Transition 𝒫 ⁡ ( s t + 1 | s t , a t ) \mathcal{P}(s_{t+1}|s_{t},a_{t}) : a deterministic update of the selected subset. If the action is select, the corresponding feature is added; otherwise the subset remains unchanged. • Reward R ⁡ ( s t , a t ) R(s_{t},a_{t}) : a hybrid reward combining downstream validation performance and LLM-based feedback. • Discount factor γ \gamma : the trade-off between short-term and long-term rewards. The objective is to maximize the expected cumulative reward: π ∗ = arg ⁡ max π ​ 𝔼 π ​ [ ∑ t = 1 T γ t − 1 ​ R ​ ( s t , a t ) ] , \pi^{*}=\arg\max_{\pi}\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}\gamma^{t-1}R(s_{t},a_{t})\right], (1) where π \pi is the policy of the RL agent and T T is the maximum number of decision steps. In our implementation, we set T = 5 ​ d T=5d to allow repeated exploration of uncertain features. Already selected features are masked out during action selection, while uncertain unselected features can be revisited through the prioritized queue. II-C 1 LLM as Decision Maker The LLM decision maker provides feature-level advice before the RL agent takes an action. Given the current selected subset S t S_{t} , the candidate feature f t f_{t} , and task information, the LLM outputs a score A LLM ​ ( f t , S t ) ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] A_{\text{LLM}}(f_{t},S_{t})\in[0,1] . A larger score indicates that the candidate feature is more likely to be useful according to domain knowledge and semantic consistency. The LLM output follows a fixed format: a numerical score, an uncertainty flag, and a short explanation. Only the numerical score is used by the RL agent, while the explanation is kept for human interpretation. The RL agent incorporates this signal by adjusting its action probabilities: π ′ ​ ( a t | s t ) ∝ π ⁡ ( a t | s t ) ⋅ exp ⁡ ( α ​ g ​ ( a t , A LLM ​ ( f t , S t ) ) ) , \pi^{\prime}(a_{t}|s_{t})\propto\pi(a_{t}|s_{t})\cdot\exp\left(\alpha g(a_{t},A_{\text{LLM}}(f_{t},S_{t}))\right), (2) where g ⁡ ( select , A ) = A g(\text{select},A)=A and g ⁡ ( skip , A ) = 1 − A g(\text{skip},A)=1-A and α \alpha controls the strength of LLM guidance. LLM advice is also used in the exploration strategy.
